name: John Ruskin
epithet: There is no wealth but life
dossier: Critic of art and of political economy. Unto This Last, quoted from the public-domain text, argues that wealth is life, that labour is the matter of economy, and that a merchant's honour is not the same as a soldier's.
voice: I ask whether this feeds life, or only the habit of gain.

works.title: Unto This Last
works.note: Public domain. Project Gutenberg, with the other essays on political economy in that volume.

entries.claim: THERE IS NO WEALTH BUT LIFE. Life, including all its powers of love, of joy, and of admiration.
entries.bears: Wealth is not a pile. It is the life that pile is supposed to serve.

entries.claim: To begin, then, with one of these necessary truisms: all economy, whether of states, households, or individuals, may be defined to be the art of managing labour.
entries.bears: Economy, at every scale, is the management of labour.

entries.claim: A bravo's trade is slaying; but the world has never respected bravos more than merchants: the reason it honours the soldier is, because he holds his life at the service of the State.
entries.bears: Honour, in the comparison, belongs to a life held for the state, not to killing or to trade as such.

entries.claim: The labour which you have paid for, does indeed become, by the act of purchase, your own labour: you have bought the hands and the time of those workers; they are, by right and justice, your own hands, your own time.
entries.bears: He grants that paid labour becomes the buyer's own, and then asks whether that buyer may spend other people's lives only for himself.

entries.claim: You may consider every pound that you spend above the just price of a work of art, as an investment in a cargo of mental quick-lime or guano, which, being laid on the fields of human nature, is to grow a harvest of pride.
entries.bears: Paying above a just price for art grows pride, not a richer common life.

entries.claim: It will be done only when the motive force, that is to say, the will or spirit of the creature, is brought to its greatest strength by its own proper fuel; namely, by the affections.
entries.bears: The strength of a life, here, is fed by affection, not by a further dose of want.
